subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The 'structure versus action' debate in sociology concerns whether:
options: Old theories are better than new ones
Society shapes individuals or individuals shape society
questions.explain: The structure-action debate asks whether social structures determine behaviour or whether individuals actively create society.

questions.q: A key criticism of functionalism is that it:
options: Rejects the idea of shared values
Tends to ignore conflict and inequality, seeing society as too harmonious
questions.explain: Critics argue functionalism overstates consensus and harmony and neglects conflict and inequality.

questions.q: Marxist feminists differ from radical feminists because they emphasise that women's oppression is linked mainly to:
questions.explain: Marxist feminists argue women's oppression is tied to capitalism and the economic system, not patriarchy alone.

questions.q: Postmodernists argue that, compared with the past, identities today are:
options: More fluid, fragmented and chosen by individuals
questions.explain: Postmodernists argue modern identities are more fluid and fragmented, with individuals constructing identity from many sources.

questions.q: In Marxist theory, 'false class consciousness' means that workers:
options: Have no social class at all
Fail to recognise their true exploited position under capitalism
Fully understand their exploitation and revolt
questions.explain: False class consciousness is the failure of the proletariat to recognise their real exploited interests under capitalism.

questions.q: Which thinker is most associated with the idea that religion can be the 'opium of the people'?
questions.explain: Marx described religion as the 'opium of the people', arguing it dulls the pain of exploitation and discourages revolt.

questions.q: Marxism is best described as a:
options: Conflict theory based on class division and inequality
Consensus theory based on shared values
questions.explain: Marxism is a conflict theory focusing on class division between owners and workers under capitalism.

questions.q: 'Non-participant observation' means the researcher:
options: Joins in fully with the group's activities
Observes the group without taking part in their activities
questions.explain: In non-participant observation the researcher watches the group without joining in their activities.

questions.q: Durkheim used the term 'anomie' to describe a state of:
options: Strong shared values and clear rules
Normlessness, where social norms are unclear or breaking down
questions.explain: Durkheim used 'anomie' to mean a condition of normlessness in which social norms become weak or unclear.

questions.q: In Marxist theory, the 'bourgeoisie' are:
options: The ruling class who own the means of production
questions.explain: The bourgeoisie are the capitalist ruling class who own the means of production and profit from workers' labour.

questions.q: Liberal feminists believe gender equality can best be achieved through:
options: Gradual reform, such as changes to laws and attitudes
questions.explain: Liberal feminists favour gradual reform through changes in law, education and attitudes to achieve equality.

questions.q: A common criticism of Marxism is that it:
options: Places too much emphasis on class and the economy, neglecting other factors
questions.explain: Critics argue Marxism is too economically deterministic, overstating class and underplaying factors like gender and ethnicity.

questions.q: Which theory focuses most on small-scale, face-to-face interaction and the meanings people give to behaviour?
questions.explain: Interactionism is a micro, social-action approach focusing on how people interact and interpret meanings.

questions.q: Marx argued that the economic 'base' of society shapes the 'superstructure', meaning:
options: Ideas have no connection to the economy
The way production is organised influences institutions like law, education and religion
questions.explain: Marx argued the economic base (the mode of production) shapes the superstructure of institutions and ideas in society.

questions.q: Radical feminists differ from liberal feminists mainly because they argue:
options: Gender equality can be achieved through gradual reform
Patriarchy is deep-rooted and requires far-reaching change
Class is the only form of inequality
questions.explain: Radical feminists see patriarchy as fundamental and requiring radical change, whereas liberal feminists favour gradual reform.

questions.q: A 'macro' approach in sociology is one that:
options: Focuses on the whole structure of society and large-scale forces
questions.explain: Macro approaches, such as functionalism and Marxism, focus on large-scale social structures rather than individuals.

questions.q: Feminist sociologists argue that society is shaped by:
options: Patriarchy, a system of male dominance
questions.explain: Feminists argue society is patriarchal, organised in ways that advantage men over women.

questions.q: Functionalism is best described as a theory based on:
options: Consensus, viewing society as parts working together for stability
The rejection of all social order
questions.explain: Functionalism is a consensus theory: it sees society as made of interconnected parts working together to maintain stability.

questions.q: Modernity, as a period, is generally associated with:
options: A complete rejection of all knowledge
Belief in science, progress and reason
questions.explain: Modernity is linked to the rise of science, reason and belief in social progress, contrasted with postmodernity.

questions.q: 'Validity' in research refers to whether:
options: The data gives a true, authentic picture of what it claims to measure
The results can be repeated to get the same findings
questions.explain: Validity is about whether data is genuine and accurately reflects reality, giving a true picture.

questions.q: Interactionists argue that society is best understood by studying:
options: The meanings and labels people create through everyday interaction
questions.explain: Interactionists focus on how individuals interpret situations and create meaning through everyday face-to-face interaction.

questions.q: In Marxist theory, the 'proletariat' are:
options: The owners of the means of production
The working class who sell their labour
questions.explain: The proletariat are the working class who, owning no means of production, must sell their labour to the bourgeoisie.
